correctness.rationale: The published polarity description gives the vertex set. Maximizing a linear functional over the intersection ball shows that an exposed one-dimensional face has exactly \(k-1\) forced signed coordinates and a two-way tie for the last coordinate, hence adjacency is exactly one signed-coordinate exchange. Each edge can increase the number of correct target signed coordinates by at most one; if supports agree and the vertices differ, the first edge must leave the support and an extra step is necessary. The explicit exchange chains attain both lower bounds. Counting same-sign, opposite-sign and exchanged coordinates gives the shell formula. A fresh independent breadth-first replay on \((d,k)=(4,2)\) and \((5,3)\) matched every tested pair distance; the frozen checker was read and exhausts all cases through dimension seven.
correctness.risk: The theorem treats integer \(k\) and the ordinary unweighted one-skeleton metric only.

value.rationale: These are natural norm balls motivated by optimization, and their skeleton is a current signed-Johnson graph used in coding/combinatorial geometry. An exact all-pairs metric, diameter and distance distribution provide structural navigational information not contained in the published face enumeration.
value.risk: The result is limited to ordinary graph distance for integer-parameter members of the family.

final_claim: For \(P_{d,k}=(kB_1^d)\cap[-1,1]^d\) with \(1\le k<d\), the vertices are the \(k\)-sparse sign vectors, two vertices are adjacent exactly when their dot product is \(k-1\), and the all-pairs graph distance is \(k-a(u,v)\) when the supports differ and \(k-a(u,v)+1\) for unequal vertices with identical support. Consequently the diameter is \(k+1\) and the stated closed distance-shell formula holds.
limitations: Integer \(1\le k<d\) is the nontrivial regime; the cube endpoint \(k=d\) is separately Hamming.
The full Takhanov-Yun 2026 text was inaccessible in this run and remains an originality residual risk.
